archetype.name: Dual-Threat (sack-prone)
archetype.definition: A mobile passer who does real damage downfield and with his legs, but holds the ball into sacks often enough to give back much of what he creates.

report.headline: The throws are back; the sacks, fumbles and missing touchdowns still cap him
report.take:
Watson's 2026 is the best version of him Cleveland has seen, and still a long way from the Houston version. His 7.33 yards per attempt ranks 18th of 54, and he is beating the league's per-attempt averages across the board (+0.51 YPA, +2.5 completion points). Set that against a 2024 in which his EPA per play ranked 54th of 60 and this is a real rebound. Yet his EPA per dropback sits at -0.003, 28th, barely above the qualifier average. The gap between good passing and mediocre dropbacks has one main cause: sacks.

He has been sacked on 11.3% of dropbacks (45th of 54), and 41.8% of his pressures end in a sack, 39th of 42. That is not new. His pressure-to-sack rate has ranked near the bottom in every season since 2018, including a 0.541 mark in 2022. The pressure itself is only middling (24.5% of dropbacks, 30th of 42). His line does allow the most hits in the league, but he converts pressure into sacks at a rate few quarterbacks match. The damage clusters on third down: 13 of his sacks, a 30.2% conversion rate, and an average of 8 yards to go. When he does let it rip, it works. Throws of 10+ air yards return 0.42 EPA per attempt, intermediate throws 0.391, deep balls 0.462. Scrambles add 0.33 EPA apiece with 10 first downs in 26 tries.

The recent box scores hide a shift. Over the last three games he has averaged 314.7 passing yards, with a 0.7 CPOE and 8.21 YPA. That looks like a breakout. But his aggressiveness fell to 5.6%, 5.1% and 7.5% in those games, after running 10% to 21% earlier, so the yards come from a shorter, higher-completion game that piles up volume without finishing drives. He has zero passing touchdowns in that stretch, and his 2.4% TD rate ranks 41st. His EPA per dropback (-0.007) is no better than his season mark. Add three lost fumbles (50th of 54) and eight turnover-worthy fumbles, and the yardage isn't turning into points.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the offense lets him keep the efficient downfield element while the quick game protects him. The TD drought on 300-yard volume should ease, since red-zone CPOE (1.7) is fine and the zero is partly a small-sample cold streak. The sack rate will not fix itself; it is who he has been for nearly a decade.

strengths.title: Real damage beyond ten yards
strengths.body: Once the ball travels 10+ air yards he has been one of the more productive passers in the league per throw, with intermediate and deep EPA both well above anything the short game produces. The completion rates there are ordinary, so this comes from chunk gains, not accuracy luck. It is sustainable if the scheme keeps calling it. The concern is that recent game plans have pulled away from it.

strengths.title: Scrambles are a weapon
strengths.body: His legs add a steady floor: 29.6 rushing yards a game ranks 4th among quarterbacks. Scrambles are where the value lives, at a positive EPA per scramble with frequent first downs. Designed runs are a different story, at 2.64 yards per carry with a 28% stuff rate, though they have produced both rushing TDs. Expect the scramble value to hold; it has been part of his game since Houston.

strengths.title: Tight end Fannin as the engine
strengths.body: Harold Fannin Jr. is the most productive target in the offense by a wide margin, at 0.358 EPA per target. The wide receivers all sit near 0.1. Watson's best football runs through that connection, and it gives him a reliable outlet in the middle range.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He takes sacks at one of the highest rates in the league, and that alone drags good per-attempt passing down to average per-dropback value. Some of it is the line: the offense is hit more than any in football. But his pressure-to-sack rate has been bottom-tier in nearly every season since 2018, so this is a trait, not a slump. Expect it to persist, with third downs absorbing most of the damage.

concerns.title: Yards without touchdowns
concerns.body: Three straight 300-yard games have produced no passing scores. His season TD rate ranks 41st, while his yardage ranks 15th. The recent dip in aggressiveness explains part of it: shorter throws move the chains between the 20s but don't finish. Some regression toward more touchdowns is likely, but he needs to push the ball again to get there.

concerns.title: Ball security in the pocket
concerns.body: Three lost fumbles rank near the bottom of the position, and the eight turnover-worthy fumbles say the lost count could easily be worse. This ties directly to holding the ball into contact, so it travels with the sack problem rather than being random.

trend.note: He opened with three positive-EPA games in four, then cratered against the Jets (8 sacks, -10.6 EPA) and Baltimore. Since Week 7 the yardage has surged on a conservative, high-completion approach, but per-dropback value and scoring haven't followed.

nextGame.headline: Bottom-five pass defense at home after a bye
nextGame.body:
Las Vegas is among the softest pass defenses in the league. It ranks 28th in pass EPA allowed, last in success rate allowed, and last against short throws, and it gives up 2.5 touchdowns a game to quarterbacks (31st). That lines up neatly with how Cleveland has been playing lately: a heavy diet of short completions should keep moving the chains, and the red zone is where the Raiders have bled points. The risk sits with the rush: the Raiders hit quarterbacks at the 7th-highest rate, which is the exact pressure Watson tends to turn into sacks. He also comes off 14 days of rest.

Availability needs a check. The site's status flag lists him as Out, but his only practice report is from Week 9, the game Shedeur Sanders started. He then played every snap in Week 10, and the depth chart had him at QB1 as of Nov. 17. Confirm his status before kickoff. On the other side, edge rusher Kwity Paye (neck, 61% of snaps) is questionable and DT Thomas Booker IV sat last week; missing either thins the hit rate that threatens Watson most. Brock Bowers' ankle matters for script: without him, a Raiders offense that ranks 31st running the ball has less to keep pace with.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs. league-worst short defense
keyMatchups.body: Raiders opponents have found more value on short throws than against any other defense. Watson's recent game plans have leaned on exactly those throws. This is the matchup where the conservative approach can finally produce efficiency, not just volume.

keyMatchups.title: Raiders' hit rate vs. his sack habit
keyMatchups.body: Las Vegas gets to quarterbacks often, and Watson converts pressure to sacks at a bottom-tier rate. If Paye plays, drive-killing third-down sacks are the main way this matchup goes wrong.

keyMatchups.title: WR2 and backs open; Fannin's lane tighter
keyMatchups.body: The Raiders have been gashed by second receivers and lead backs. Tight ends get a larger share of targets against them than league norm but produce little per play. Spreading it to Concepcion or Boston and Judkins may pay more than forcing it to Fannin.

nextGame.watch: Whether he finally throws touchdowns against a defense that allows them freely, or stalls again in the red zone and on third down.

restOfSeason.body:
The baseline is a quarterback who throws for well above the league average per game and adds real rushing value. His ceiling is limited by sacks and fumbles that have followed him his whole career. The touchdown rate should climb back toward his red-zone efficiency, which isn't poor, so expect something like 0.9 to 1.4 passing scores a game rather than the recent zeros. The 300-yard run is partly game plan and partly soft opponents (Tennessee, Houston), so 230 to 290 yards a game is a fairer expectation.

What won't regress is the sack rate: three to five a game is the realistic band given his history and a line that allows the most hits in football. If the coaches restore the downfield shots that drove his early-season EPA while keeping the quick game, his per-dropback value can move into the top half of the league. If not, he stays a volume passer who helps fantasy lineups more than the scoreboard.

confidence.note: Nine starts is a solid sample, but his availability is unclear.
